humanities_role_explanation: The benchmark targets domain-specific competence in rhetorical analysis of historical documents, evaluating whether models can accurately distinguish and segment fine-grained components of classical rhetoric (Salutatio, Petitio, and Conclusio) inside 18th-century Swedish and English petitioning texts.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: The models process text transcriptions of 18th-century historical petitions.
analytical_tasks_explanation: The tasks require token-level span extraction and annotation of classical rhetorical structures (information extraction and stylistic analysis) as well as self-assessing task difficulty (calibration and uncertainty).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: The evaluation dataset is specifically tailored to the rhetorical segmentation of historical petitions rather than broad, multi-domain benchmarks.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates GPT-4, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Mixtral 8x22B, Mistral 7B, LLaMA-3 70B, and LLaMA-3 8B.

quantitative_metrics.note: Employs token-level precision, recall, F1-score, mean token-level Levenshtein edit distance, Mean Error (ME) for difficulty ratings, and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.

summary: The paper investigates the capability of LLMs to automatically annotate classical rhetorical structures in 18th-century Swedish and English petitions using few-shot prompting. The authors evaluate model accuracy against a human-annotated gold standard and analyze whether models can successfully calibrate their self-estimated difficulty scores with human annotations.
key_findings: While models perform exceptionally well on the formulaic Salutatio (often scoring in the high 90s for F1), the Petitio and Conclusio segments are significantly more challenging, especially for smaller models and Swedish data. Additionally, models systematically underestimate the annotation difficulty of documents and show weak or negative correlation with human-perceived difficulty ratings.
facets_explanation: The Swedish petitions were transcribed by a historian, while the English ones were sourced from a digitised archive. For rhetorical span annotation, each document was labeled by two of three project annotators, with disagreements systematically resolved through batch-wise discussions to establish consistent guidelines. A difficulty score (0-2) was also assigned to each document based on the degree of consensus and interpretive challenges experienced during annotation.
